slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now; it should fund the software business, which nears breakeven within current cash
Quick commerce grows fast, but no operator has made it pay
–	Zipcart loses $1.90 an order; QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities
On our customers' benchmarks, every Parcelbird Now order loses money
–	At the median site, an order loses $6.17 after site costs
–	The plan's $2.02 profit vanishes at a median basket or rider pace
The Columbus pop-up did worse, and few of its customers stayed
–	Each pop-up order lost $12.57 after site costs
–	Only 22% still ordered in month three, at $173 each to win
The plan breaks the 12-month runway rule; a one-site pilot proves little
–	The $9.5M plan leaves $2.5M at month 18, half the floor
The software business nears breakeven within current cash
–	ARR nears the $11M breakeven by end-2028, with $5.4M left
–	Four gates guard the runway and set terms for dark stores

slides.title: Resetting either basket size or rider pace to the median turns the plan's $2.02 profit per order into a loss

Resetting either basket size or rider pace to the median turns the plan's $2.02 profit per order into a loss
Contribution per order after dark-store costs, $, founders' plan with one input reset to the 2025 median
The plan has almost no margin for error
▪	Basket size: the plan's $45 is above the best site's $42; the median basket is $34
▪	Rider pace: the plan's 3.5 orders an hour is above every site in the 1.9–3.0 range
▪	Volume and promotions: each alone leaves the plan only just above zero
▪	Break-even pace: at the median basket, riders must deliver 3.75 orders an hour just to cover per-order costs
1  Each bar resets one plan input to the 2025 median and keeps the others; 'All four' is the median site (p. 8)

slides.title: A one-site pilot is no cheap test: it would use about $2.6M in its first year without proving the plan

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Economics    3 Pop-up    4 Cash    5 Software
A one-site pilot is no cheap test: it would use about $2.6M in its first year without proving the plan
First-year cash cost of one permanent Columbus dark store, $ thousands, team estimate
capex for one dark store (founders' plan)
fixed cost for a year: rent, staff, utilities (benchmark)
per-order losses: $2.67 an order × 900 orders a day for a full year
first-year cash cost, before customer acquisition
The estimate is a floor, not a ceiling
▪	One permanent site at the benchmark median of 900 orders a day for a full year, a level the pop-up's 280 a day did not reach
▪	Per-order economics at the benchmark median: a loss of $2.67 before site costs
▪	Capex of $0.6M and a fixed cost of $1.15M a year, as in the founders' plan
▪	Customer acquisition and launch marketing are left out, so the true cost is higher
Over a third of the $7.2M above the runway floor, to test a basket and pace no site has reached
1  At the pop-up's 280 orders a day and $6.21 loss an order the per-order losses would be smaller, but the site would show nothing about density
Sources: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis
